question: Can a learned hierarchy of scalar bottlenecks faithfully and usefully visualize the joint effects of every variable in an arbitrary high-dimensional continuous black-box function, and do the approximation theorem, grouping heuristic, numerical evidence, visual presentation, and released artifact support that claim?

key_findings.claim: The paper's distinctive practical contribution is a linked sequence of low-dimensional views, not literally one plot containing every original variable.
key_findings.evidence: At the top level, IANN fits f(x) approximately as g(x_j,h(x_without_j)) and plots the learned two-input surface g. OVH recursively decomposes the scalar latent h into d-1 surfaces; DASH first replaces disjoint input groups by learned linear combinations and needs p-1 surfaces. The views collectively expose a path through all variables, but interpretation still requires moving between separately scaled latent panels.

key_findings.claim: Theorem 2.1 is false for d at least three, so it cannot justify universal scalar-bottleneck visualization or the recursive OVH construction.
key_findings.evidence: For d=3 and j=1 take f(x,y,z)=(1-x)y+xz. If f were uniformly within epsilon of g(x,h(y,z)), restrict continuous h to the square boundary. An equivariant homeomorphism from S^1 to that boundary and the one-dimensional Borsuk-Ulam theorem give antipodal p and q=1-p with h(p)=h(q). Comparing the common g value at x=0 forces |p_y-q_y|<2 epsilon, and at x=1 forces |p_z-q_z|<2 epsilon. Because p is on the boundary, one of those gaps is exactly one. Hence epsilon must exceed one half, contradicting the theorem's claim for every positive epsilon. Continuity of g is not needed for this counterexample.

anchors.section: Recursive use of Theorem 2.1 for OVH

key_findings.claim: The supplemental proof contains a circular discretization step that explains, but does not repair, the false theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The official arXiv source bundle preserves Appendix D as commented source. It builds, for each grid resolution n, an injective polygonal path H through grid-cell centers, defines g(x_j,t)=f(x_j,H(t)), extends H inverse to a continuous h by Tietze, and then invokes uniform continuity. The needed continuity radius belongs to the n-dependent extension h_n, but the proof subsequently chooses n from that radius without proving a uniform lower bound or a valid fixed point. The resulting n-depends-on-delta(n) loop is exposed concretely by the counterexample.

anchors.section: Theorem 2.1, proof deferred to Appendix D

key_findings.claim: The claimed universal DASH reduction is independently invalid when the learned number of groups p is smaller than d.
key_findings.evidence: DASH maps each disjoint group to one scalar linear combination v_i and then treats f as a function of v. For p<d that map is generally non-injective, so an arbitrary f need not be constant on its fibers and need not define any function of v at all. The text's statement that Theorem 2.1 applies merely because each v_i ranges over a closed interval skips this necessary factorization assumption. The construction can be a useful fitted approximation when its test error is small, but it is not a universal consequence of the theorem.

anchors.section: Claimed application of Theorem 2.1 to DASH

key_findings.claim: The learned scalar latents are not canonical explanatory variables, and their non-identifiability is substantially broader than the paper acknowledges.
key_findings.evidence: The paper notes that additive or multiplicative constants can be moved between h and g. More generally, any homeomorphism phi of the scalar latent range yields the identical predictor after replacing h by phi composed with h and g(x,t) by g(x,phi inverse(t)). This can reverse or nonlinearly warp every latent axis and change apparent slopes, curvature, spacing, and linearity without changing f. Recursive levels compound the ambiguity, so an accurate surface is a coordinate-dependent visualization rather than a uniquely identified scientific mechanism.

anchors.section: Section 3.1, stated non-uniqueness of g and h

key_findings.claim: The gradient-projection ordering score is a heuristic necessary-condition check, not a sufficient or stability-certified structure discovery method.
key_findings.evidence: Under an exact IANN factorization, gradients with respect to the remaining coordinates are collinear when selected coordinates vary, motivating a PCA residual score and greedy ordering. The reverse implication is not proved, finite differences and Latin-hypercube sampling introduce approximation error, and the relative score normalizes by average squared gradient length without a stated zero-gradient safeguard. No theorem, bootstrap interval, perturbation test, or seed-stability analysis shows that the recovered order or DASH groups are identifiable.

key_findings.claim: Held-out predictive fidelity is a useful guardrail, but the paper never defines its r-squared metric and the official code implements mutually inconsistent nonstandard scores.
key_findings.evidence: The article repeatedly labels a large random-input score as test r-squared without a formula. At artifact commit e687a3e7becb6270c2f04bfc2b2e51d6fcbc3556, OH_eg.py, DASH_eg.py, and add_eg1.py use 1-SSE/sum(y squared), an uncentered denominator, whereas computer_sim_group.py and IANNModel.score use 1-Var(error)/Var(y), which is explained variance and ignores a constant prediction bias. Neither is necessarily standard 1-SSE/SST, so printed percentages cannot be interpreted or reproduced as one consistent statistic.

key_findings.claim: The reported fits are numerically high, but most examples are constructed to match the proposed hierarchy and the only main real benchmark is almost linear over its domain.
key_findings.evidence: The five-dimensional quadratic is exactly compatible with OVH and scores 99.97%; the nine-dimensional synthetic function is explicitly built from three disjoint linear groups and scores 99.98%. The borehole example scores 99.99%, but a linear model already scores 94.68%, and three members of one four-variable DASH group receive coefficients near zero. The harmonic wave is nonlinear and physically legible, yet it too has a known exact compatible OVH expression. These are demonstrations, not broad comparative evidence that the method discovers stable semantics in arbitrary functions.

key_findings.claim: The simulation case in the supplement evaluates IANN against a learned surrogate, not directly against the physical simulator, and does not propagate surrogate uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: The main paper says the additional physical example first fits a surrogate to a complex strain-loaded material simulation. The supplement reports 1,000 simulations, a cross-validated surrogate r-squared of 99.30%, then trains IANN on 35,000 surrogate-generated points and evaluates one million points against that same surrogate, with top-level scores up to 99.75%. This establishes compression fidelity to the surrogate conditional on its errors; it does not validate the displayed structure against new simulator runs or compose the two approximation errors.

anchors.section: Section 5.2, reference to Appendix C examples

key_findings.claim: No experiment tests whether people understand the linked surfaces better, faster, or more accurately than existing visual explanations.
key_findings.evidence: The ICE/PD comparison is one qualitative harmonic-wave illustration, and ALE is omitted because it resembles PD in that independent-input example. The remaining evidence reports fit scores and visually compares learned surfaces to known formulas. There is no user study, task accuracy, time-to-insight, explanation stability, calibrated trust, or systematic comparison against PD, ICE, ALE, trellis, active-subspace, additive-index, or topological visualization baselines.

key_findings.claim: The visual design communicates the hierarchy but is not presentation-robust at paper scale.
key_findings.evidence: All main visuals were inspected. Figures 3, 6, 8, 9, and 10 place several static 3D panels with small axes, ticks, coefficient labels, and legends on one page; perspective and occlusion make slopes and extrema viewpoint-dependent. Figure 4's claim that the 3D IANN surface clarifies ICE is not perception-tested. The paper itself proposes interactive rotation, heatmaps, shaded rendering, linked points, and sliders as future work, implicitly identifying the missing interactions needed for dependable reading.

key_findings.claim: The recommended choose-the-largest-acceptable-hyperparameter procedure risks validation leakage if the displayed test score is reused for selection.
key_findings.evidence: For DASH grouping, the supplement selects the largest grouping threshold eta that retains an acceptably high test r-squared; the main text similarly tells users to try DASH and fall back to OVH when its test r-squared is not acceptably high. No separate validation and final test split is specified. Reusing the same large random sample to choose structure, order, threshold, or architecture and then reporting its score makes that sample validation data rather than an unbiased final test.

anchors.section: Section 2.2, adequacy measured on a test set

key_findings.claim: The current method is explicitly unsafe for correlated observational inputs because it learns and displays unsupported rectangular-domain behavior.
key_findings.evidence: Training uses space-filling designs over a Cartesian box, which is sensible when every simulator input combination is meaningful. For observational predictors concentrated near a lower-dimensional support, the same procedure queries sparse or impossible combinations. The conclusion acknowledges that this extrapolation can render interpretations unreliable; unlike the same author's ALE predecessor, IANN supplies no support-aware sampling or conditional-domain constraint.

key_findings.claim: The first-party artifact establishes provenance but is not a functioning modern reproduction package.
key_findings.evidence: The article links a Python package; the first-party repository was audited at commit e687a3e7becb6270c2f04bfc2b2e51d6fcbc3556. setup.py declares Python at least 3.5 but no dependencies despite TensorFlow, Keras, SciPy, scikit-learn, pyDOE, pandas, SALib, and other imports. Installed package imports are non-relative, pytest fails during collection with ModuleNotFoundError for regressor, IANNModel ignores its dim argument and hard-codes five, np.int is removed in modern NumPy, and paths are partly Windows-specific. Although several separate BIANN prototype scripts set seeds, the principal IANN examples and IANNModel do not, and no deterministic end-to-end command or raw result logs reproduce the paper tables.

anchors.section: Supplementary Materials, Python package for IANN

key_findings.claim: Later citations do not currently provide independent confirmation, correction, or a direct successor.
key_findings.evidence: Primary-text tracing through 2026-08-23 found three later citations: Bivariate DeepKriging gives one generic interpretability sentence and uses Shapley analysis; a 2024 bioinspired actor-critic paper gives one background sentence before developing Levy-Brown exploration; and a 2026 plant response-surface paper cites the work while fitting quadratic central-composite designs. None runs IANN, reproduces a figure, extends the hierarchy, or analyzes Theorem 2.1. The closest later architectural alternatives, KAN/KAN 2.0 and asKAN, do not cite the target and should be treated as independent competitors.

method.core_idea: Replace a high-dimensional scalar black-box function by a learned sequence of two-input response surfaces: at each level, expose one original variable or one disjoint linear input group and compress all remaining information into a scalar latent bottleneck that is decomposed at the next level.
method.mechanism: A customized feedforward network jointly learns g and scalar h under mean squared error. OVH nests d-1 bottlenecks according to a greedy ordering of original variables. DASH prepends a constrained linear layer, learns disjoint active groups v_i=beta_i-transpose x_Ji, and nests only p-1 bottlenecks. Candidate orders and groups are selected from collinearity of gradients evaluated on Latin-hypercube samples; training uses a boundary-augmented Latin hypercube. Each learned g_i is rendered as a 3D surface or heatmap, and a large random-input fit score is used as the fidelity gate.
assumptions: The target is a deterministic continuous scalar function over a meaningful Cartesian product of bounded input intervals, or a surrogate that can be queried throughout that box.
A scalar latent at every OVH level, or disjoint linear group scalars in DASH, can approximate the target sufficiently well with the chosen finite network.
Gradient evaluations or finite differences are available and stable enough for the projection-ordering heuristic.
The fitted latent coordinates and learned linear combinations are sufficiently stable and semantically meaningful for visual interpretation despite their non-identifiability.
A high global random-sample fit score is an adequate proxy for local visual fidelity and explanation reliability.
For DASH with p smaller than d, the response approximately factors through the learned non-injective group map; this is an empirical structural assumption, not a universal theorem.

techniques.role: Compress the variables omitted from one view into one learned coordinate h so the outer function can be shown as a two-input surface.
Recursively expose one original variable per level, producing d-1 linked surfaces.
Learn disjoint linear input groups before the hierarchy to reduce the number of visual levels from d-1 to p-1.
Rank candidate exposed variables or groups by how nearly collinear the remaining-coordinate gradients are across changes in the candidates.
Augment maximin Latin-hypercube interior points with coordinate-boundary projections for space-filling network training.
Train every level simultaneously against the original response so approximation errors are not explicitly cascaded through separately fitted stages.
Render outer functions as 3D surfaces or heatmaps and read the latent effect through subsequent panels.

evaluations.setting: Four-dimensional harmonic wave f=x1 sin((2 pi/x2)x3+x4), nonhierarchical singled-variable sweep
evaluations.metric: Author-labeled test r-squared on random box samples
evaluations.result: Singling out x1 scores 99.80%; the x2, x3, and x4 alternatives score 80.47%, 72.76%, and 83.67%, respectively, motivating x1 as the first level.
evaluations.baseline: The four candidate exposed variables are compared with one another; no PD, ICE, ALE, active-subspace, or other model fit is quantitatively benchmarked.

evaluations.setting: Five-dimensional synthetic quadratic with an exact OVH-compatible expression
evaluations.metric: Author-labeled test r-squared and qualitative recovery of linear/quadratic structure
evaluations.result: 99.97%; four linked panels visually recover the known quadratic outer response and linear inner latents.

evaluations.setting: Nine-dimensional synthetic function explicitly composed from three disjoint linear groups
evaluations.metric: Author-labeled test r-squared and learned coefficient ratios
evaluations.result: 99.98%; DASH recovers the three true groups and approximately proportional coefficients, reducing eight OVH panels to two DASH panels.
evaluations.baseline: Exact generating formula and an asserted eight-panel OVH alternative; no competing group-discovery method.

evaluations.setting: Eight-dimensional borehole response surface over standard bounded ranges
evaluations.metric: Author-labeled test r-squared on one million random points, runtime, and total sensitivity indices
evaluations.result: DASH uses 34,000 training points, takes 96 seconds for ordering and 245 seconds for fitting, and reports 99.99%; constrained orders span 99.94%-99.99%.
evaluations.baseline: A linear model reports 94.68%, and SALib sensitivity indices provide a qualitative importance check.

evaluations.setting: Harmonic wave with the full three-level OVH hierarchy
evaluations.metric: Author-labeled test r-squared and qualitative comparison with amplitude, phase, and wavelength semantics
evaluations.result: 99.95%; the linked panels visually match the known analytic hierarchy.
evaluations.baseline: Known formula; DASH is said to find no useful nontrivial disjoint group.

evaluations.setting: Supplemental three-input strain-loaded material potential-energy simulator via an intermediate neural surrogate
evaluations.metric: Ten-fold surrogate cross-validation score and IANN test score against surrogate-generated values
evaluations.result: The surrogate reports 99.30%; IANN is trained on 35,000 surrogate samples and the best exposed variable reports 99.75%, with alternatives around 97.42%-97.52%.
evaluations.baseline: The learned surrogate, not fresh simulator evaluations; no uncertainty propagation or competing explanation method.

limitations: The universal approximation theorem is false for d at least three, and the official supplemental proof contains a circular n-dependent uniform-continuity step.
DASH with p smaller than d needs an unproved approximate factorization through a non-injective linear-group map.
Scalar latent axes are invariant under arbitrary homeomorphic reparameterizations, so visual slopes, curvature, spacing, and even orientation are not identified.
Predictive r-squared measures output fidelity, not whether the hierarchy is comprehensible, causal, stable, or scientifically faithful.
No human study, explanation task, stability analysis, ablation, or systematic quantitative visualization baseline is included.
Most demonstrations exactly match the proposed architecture; the borehole case is already close to linear.
Training and evaluation cover rectangular input boxes and can extrapolate badly for correlated observational predictors.
Gradient collinearity is used as if it diagnosed hierarchical structure, but only a forward necessary-condition argument is supplied.
Static multi-panel 3D figures suffer from small labels, occlusion, perspective dependence, and cross-panel latent-scale ambiguity.
The first-party code has broken imports, undeclared dependencies, removed NumPy APIs, a hard-coded dimension, no deterministic paper-run scripts, and inconsistent fit metrics.
failure_modes: A target such as f(x,y,z)=(1-x)y+xz cannot pass through one continuous scalar h(y,z) below uniform error one half, directly falsifying the basic guarantee.
Distinct points collapsed by h or by a DASH group projection can require incompatible response curves as the exposed coordinate changes.
A high average fit score can coexist with large errors in a small, safety-critical, boundary, derivative-sensitive, or visually salient region.
Nearly zero gradients make the relative projection score undefined or noise-dominated and can produce arbitrary variable orders or spurious groups.
Different random initializations can learn homeomorphically warped or substantively different latents while achieving indistinguishable global fit.
Using the same random sample to choose order, grouping threshold, architecture, and reported score overstates generalization.
A highly accurate IANN-to-surrogate fit can faithfully visualize surrogate artifacts rather than the underlying simulator.
Static 3D viewpoints can hide folds, crossings, extrema, or interaction changes and invite interpretation from a projection artifact.
The released package fails before training in a modern clean environment, preventing an independent paper reproduction without code repair.
reusable_insights: Treat low-dimensional visualization as a lossy communication channel: certify collisions and conditional-curve disagreement, not just aggregate prediction error.
A linked hierarchy of two-input views is a useful interface pattern even when it is presented as an empirical approximation rather than a universal representation theorem.
Separate structural discovery, model selection, and final fidelity evaluation into distinct data splits, then report local and worst-region error alongside one global score.
Canonicalize scalar latents with explicit constraints such as orientation, quantile scaling, smoothness, monotonicity where justified, and repeated-seed alignment before comparing panels.
Attach uncertainty and support density to every surface so unsupported observational regions and surrogate-error amplification are visible.
Use interactive linked brushing: moving an original input should highlight the corresponding locations on every latent panel and allow direct inspection of preimages collapsed by a bottleneck.
Test interpretability with user tasks against ICE, ALE, active-subspace plots, additive-index models, and symbolic or spline alternatives rather than inferring it from a high fit score.
For group discovery, bootstrap gradients and report group/order frequencies, eigengaps, zero-gradient handling, and sensitivity to finite-difference step size.
Artifact checks should define the metric once, use package-relative imports, pin a clean environment, expose deterministic commands, and preserve raw run outputs.
open_questions: What is the smallest bottleneck dimension needed to approximate a target to a specified uniform or conditional-curve error, and can topology give computable lower bounds?
Can scalar-latent collision tests detect before training that conditional response curves cannot share one code?
Which canonicalization makes independently trained latent hierarchies comparable without claiming that one arbitrary coordinate is scientific truth?
Can DASH group and order recovery be made statistically consistent under noisy function or gradient queries?
How should local, boundary, derivative, monotonicity, and interaction fidelity be summarized alongside global prediction error?
Do users make more accurate scientific inferences with linked IANN surfaces than with coordinated ICE/ALE, active-subspace, KAN, or topological views?
Can a support-aware variant learn only on the observational data manifold and refuse extrapolative panels?
How should simulator and surrogate uncertainty propagate through every latent level and surface?
Would a balanced tree with two-dimensional or adaptive-width bottlenecks give a better depth-versus-fidelity tradeoff than the scalar chain?
Can interactive preimage inspection reveal when many physically distinct input states occupy the same latent coordinate?
Which parts of the printed numerical results survive under one standard r-squared definition and a clean deterministic artifact rerun?

competitive_landscape.title: Peeking Inside the Black Box: Visualizing Statistical Learning with Plots of Individual Conditional Expectation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-target foundational conditional-effect visualization that preserves heterogeneous per-instance response curves.
competitive_landscape.difference: ICE retains one curve for every fixed omitted-input configuration and can become cluttered; IANN learns a scalar ordering of those configurations and turns the family into a surface, introducing compression error and latent non-identifiability.

competitive_landscape.title: Visualizing the Effects of Predictor Variables in Black Box Supervised Learning Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Same-author predecessor introducing accumulated local effects for black-box predictor visualization.
competitive_landscape.difference: ALE estimates low-order effects without extrapolating far outside correlated-data support; IANN targets a full linked joint hierarchy but assumes a meaningful rectangular domain and explicitly lacks the correlated-observational safeguard.

competitive_landscape.title: Active subspace methods in theory and practice: applications to kriging surfaces
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-target gradient-based response-surface dimension reduction and visualization through learned ridge directions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Active subspaces use eigenvectors of an expected gradient outer product and supply approximation error theory; DASH imposes disjoint groups and a recursive visual chain but offers no comparable recovery or uncertainty theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Computing active subspaces with Monte Carlo
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-target reliability analysis for estimating gradient-derived low-dimensional subspaces from samples and finite differences.
competitive_landscape.difference: It gives non-asymptotic and bootstrap guidance for sample and gradient error; IANN's related gradient-projection ordering reports neither uncertainty nor perturbation stability.

competitive_landscape.title: Explainable Neural Networks based on Additive Index Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-target intrinsically interpretable neural architecture using learned linear projections and displayed ridge functions.
competitive_landscape.difference: xNN represents the response as a regularized sum of ridge functions with overlapping projections; DASH uses disjoint projections inside a nested sequence of joint two-input surfaces.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Robust Interpretability with Self-Explaining Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-target architecture-level interpretability framework with explicit concept, faithfulness, and stability desiderata.
competitive_landscape.difference: SENN regularizes local concept-based explanations for stability and faithfulness; IANN creates global response surfaces but neither identifies latent concepts nor tests their stability.

competitive_landscape.title: Detecting Statistical Interactions from Neural Network Weights
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-target neural interaction-discovery method for arbitrary-order feature interactions.
competitive_landscape.difference: NID ranks interaction sets from an already-trained network's weights and quantitatively benchmarks recovery; IANN infers interactions visually from fitted outer-surface shape and does not benchmark interaction detection.

competitive_landscape.title: GAMI-Net: An Explainable Neural Network based on Generalized Additive Models with Structured Interactions
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-target explainable neural model with explicit main-effect and pairwise-interaction subnetworks.
competitive_landscape.difference: GAMI-Net enforces sparsity, heredity, and marginal clarity so components have more stable meanings, but limits interactions to selected pairs; IANN can display higher-order joint behavior through latents but its components are not identified.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Additive Models: Interpretable Machine Learning with Neural Nets
competitive_landscape.relationship: Explicitly discussed pre-target intrinsically interpretable neural additive model.
competitive_landscape.difference: NAM exposes one directly readable shape function per original feature and excludes interactions in its basic form; IANN's recursive bottlenecks target interactions at the cost of latent-coordinate ambiguity.

competitive_landscape.title: NODE-GAM: Neural Generalized Additive Model for Interpretable Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-target scalable neural GAM and GA2M alternative for interpretable tabular prediction.
competitive_landscape.difference: NODE-GAM and NODE-GA2M benchmark identifiable main and pairwise shapes on large datasets; IANN is a post-hoc approximating visualization of a queryable function and emphasizes linked higher-order surfaces instead.

competitive_landscape.title: ExSpliNet: An interpretable and expressive spline-based neural network
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest chronological pre-target architecture: an interpretable Kolmogorov-network and multivariate-spline model submitted seven weeks before the target's stated journal receipt.
competitive_landscape.difference: ExSpliNet supplies a valid universal approximation result and interprets internal spline or tree structure with benchmark fits; IANN's distinctive output is the linked sequence of 3D effects, but its universal scalar-bottleneck theorem is false.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Sculpting: Uncovering hierarchically modular task structure in neural networks through pruning and network analysis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Near-concurrent later work recovering hierarchical task subfunctions from trained neural networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: Neural Sculpting uses iterative pruning and graph module detection with explicit input-separability and reuse criteria on Boolean and vision tasks; IANN forces a scalar chain for continuous response surfaces and reads modules from learned panels.

competitive_landscape.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Strong post-target independent alternative for interpretable high-dimensional function approximation.
competitive_landscape.difference: KAN learns visible univariate spline functions on edges and supports symbolic inspection rather than compressing all omitted inputs into one scalar at each level; it does not cite, replicate, or extend IANN.

competitive_landscape.title: KAN 2.0: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks Meet Science
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-target scientific-discovery alternative emphasizing feature discovery, modular structure, tree conversion, and symbolic formulas.
competitive_landscape.difference: KAN 2.0 exposes and edits symbolic or modular computational structure, whereas IANN displays an approximating latent chain; KAN 2.0 provides richer scientific interfaces but is not a direct citation or replication.

competitive_landscape.title: asKAN: Active Subspace embedded Kolmogorov-Arnold Network
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest current independent conceptual alternative combining hierarchical function representation with learned active-subspace projections.
competitive_landscape.difference: asKAN inserts active-subspace detection between KANs to model ridge functions and evaluates function fit, a Poisson PDE, and sound-field reconstruction; it does not impose disjoint groups, cite IANN, or validate linked human-facing surfaces.

competitive_landscape.title: Bivariate DeepKriging for Large-scale Spatial Interpolation of Wind Fields
competitive_landscape.relationship: Verified direct later citation of IANN in a generic neural-network interpretability paragraph, added in arXiv v2 and absent from v1.
competitive_landscape.difference: Bivariate DeepKriging develops spatial basis embeddings, bootstrap uncertainty, and Shapley analysis; its 2024-added sentence neither implements IANN nor reproduces, extends, or critiques its hierarchy or theorem.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a new IANN approach that can approximate any continuous function through a scalar bottleneck, recursively visualize the joint effects of all original variables, optionally discover disjoint active groups, and make the resulting high-dimensional response understandable through linked 3D plots.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The practical architecture, OVH/DASH decompositions, gradient ordering, examples, and package are concrete. However, PD, ICE, ALE, trellis, active subspaces, additive-index neural networks, structured-interaction GAM networks, and interpretable spline architectures predate it; Theorem 2.1 is disproved by an explicit continuous counterexample; and no human or direct competitor study establishes superior comprehension.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty boundary is narrow but useful: a learned chain of scalar-bottleneck response surfaces designed specifically as a visual interface for queryable simulation or surrogate functions, plus OVH/DASH ordering and grouping heuristics. It is not the first effect plot, interaction visualization, active projection, interpretable neural architecture, or universal function representation. The false theorem must be removed from any novelty claim, and the method should be treated as an empirically gated lossy visualization whose latents require stability, support, and human-validation checks.

reviewer_notes: Identity was corrected before review: arXiv:2303.03393 is 'Interpretable Architecture Neural Networks for Function Visualization' by Shengtong Zhang and Daniel W. Apley, not the continuous-time Markov-chain title initially supplied. All 36 cached PDF pages and every main figure/table were inspected. The arXiv PDF does not typeset the promised Appendix D; the official source bundle at https://arxiv.org/src/2303.03393 preserves it as commented IANN.tex lines 1355-1425, with the circular step at lines 1410-1417. Publisher supplement landing: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/suppl/10.1080/10618600.2023.2195461. First-party artifact: https://github.com/ShengtongZhangIEMS/IANN at observed HEAD e687a3e7becb6270c2f04bfc2b2e51d6fcbc3556; syntax compiles, but clean pytest collection fails on `from regressor import IANNModel`, and package/code inspection found the dependency, dimension, NumPy, path, determinism, and metric defects summarized above. The same repository contains a BIANN balanced-tree and notebook-UI prototype implementing two future directions proposed by the paper, but it has no separate publication or independent evaluation and is not a replication. Primary-text citation tracing through 2026-08-23 found three background-only paper citations: arXiv:2307.08038, whose citation was added in v2 and is absent from v1; Neurocomputing DOI 10.1016/j.neucom.2024.127291; and Springer DOI 10.1007/s11627-026-10668-z. A same-author 2024 dissertation repeats the DeepKriging background material and is excluded from the paper count. No direct methodological extension, correction, code rerun, Figure reproduction, formal critique, or independent replication was found. Publisher and index citation counts disagree, so this review records verified works rather than asserting one total.
